content: The Curry Tree, also known as the Curry-leaf Tree (scientific name: Murraya koenigii, with synonyms Bergera koenigii and Chalcas koenigii), is a tropical to subtropical tree that belongs to the Rutaceae family. It is indigenous to India. This tree is relatively small in size, typically reaching a height of 4 to 6 meters. Its trunk can grow up to 40 centimeters in diameter. The leaves of the Curry Tree are pinnate, consisting of 11 to 21 individual leaflets. The tree produces small, white, and fragrant flowers. It also bears small, black, shiny berries that are edible; however, the seeds contained within these berries are toxic if ingested. The species name, koenigii, honors the botanist Johann Gerhard Koenig. The leaves of the Curry Tree are highly aromatic and are widely used as a culinary herb. These leaves are small, narrow, and bear a resemblance to the leaves of the Neem tree (Azadirachta indica). Due to this similarity, the Curry Tree leaves are referred to as Kari Baavu in Kannada and Karivepaku in Telugu, both of which translate to Black Neem. In Tamil and Malayalam, the leaves are called Karuveppilai, where ilai means leaves and veppilai means Neem leaf. Other regional names include Kari Patta in Hindi, Bhursunga Patra in Oriya, Kadhi Limb in Marathi, Limda in Gujarati, and Karapincha in Sinhalese. Curry leaves are commonly used as a seasoning in Indian and Sri Lankan cuisines, much like bay leaves. They are particularly popular in dishes such as curries, especially those prepared with fish or coconut milk. Fresh curry leaves have a short shelf life but can be preserved for extended periods by freezing. Dried curry leaves are also available, though their aroma is significantly less potent compared to fresh leaves. In addition to their culinary uses, Murraya koenigii exhibits a range of biological activities. These include antidiabetic, antioxidant, antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, hepatoprotective (liver-protecting), and anti-hypercholesterolemic (cholesterol-lowering) properties, among others.
